title: Arunachal on a budget: real costs for 2026
meta_description: Arunachal on a budget: what shared Sumos, homestays, permits and food really cost in 2026, sample budgets for Tawang and Ziro, and how to spend less.
summary: A budget trip to Arunachal costs about ₹2,500–4,000 per person a day if you use shared Sumos, homestays with meals and local food. Our 6-night Tawang circuit starts around ₹18,500 and 4 nights in Ziro around ₹12,000, before travel to Assam. Here is where the money goes and how to spend less.

sections.heading: What a saver day really costs
paras: Arunachal is not as cheap as Himachal or Uttarakhand, mainly because distances are long, transport runs on shared Sumos rather than state buses on most routes, and there are fewer budget beds. It is still very affordable if you travel the way local people do. A realistic saver budget is ₹2,500–4,000 per person a day for two people sharing, covering a homestay with dinner and breakfast, a share of the day's transport, lunch and small fees.

The single biggest cost is moving around. A Sumo seat from Tezpur to Tawang costs about ₹1,100–1,500 and takes a full day; a reserved taxi for a day of sightseeing in Tawang costs ₹5,500–8,000 for the whole vehicle. Rooms come next: homestays charge per person, usually including two meals, which makes them better value than hotels once you add restaurant food. All figures in this guide are indicative for 2026 and change with season; peak October and May dates cost more.

sections.heading: Getting there without overspending
paras: Almost every trip starts in Assam. Guwahati has the most flights and trains, and fares are lowest if you book three to six weeks ahead and avoid Durga Puja and Diwali weekends. For the Tawang circuit, Tezpur is closer, and a train or bus from Guwahati to Tezpur takes about 4–5 hours for a few hundred rupees; Sumos to Bomdila, Dirang and Tawang leave from Tezpur early in the morning.

For Ziro, take a train to Naharlagun, the railhead for Itanagar, or fly to Donyi Polo Airport at Hollongi. For Pasighat, Mechuka, Roing and Namdapha, Dibrugarh is the gateway, with flights and trains from across India. Overnight trains save both a night's room and a day of travel; sleeper class or 3AC from Delhi or Kolkata is the cheapest way in.
list: Guwahati to Tezpur by bus or train: about ₹200–600
Tezpur to Dirang by Sumo: about ₹700–1,000
Naharlagun to Ziro by Sumo: about ₹500–800
Dibrugarh to Pasighat by Sumo: about ₹300–500

sections.heading: Where to sleep cheaply
paras: Homestays are the backbone of budget travel in Arunachal. In Dirang, Tawang, Ziro and Mechuka, families rent rooms in their houses or in small guest buildings, usually with dinner and breakfast included at ₹1,200–2,500 per person. Rooms are simple and warm blankets are standard; bathrooms may be shared, and hot water sometimes comes by the bucket. What you gain is home food, local advice and evenings by the kitchen fire.

Town guesthouses and lodges in Bomdila, Tawang, Pasighat and Roing charge about ₹1,200–2,500 for a double, without meals. They suit travellers who want a private bathroom and do not mind eating out. Government circuit houses and inspection bungalows exist in district towns but are mainly for officials and are not reliable for tourist bookings. In Namdapha, the forest rest house at Deban is the classic budget stay, booked through the forest department in Miao.
Book ahead for October, the Ziro Festival of Music in late September, and Torgya in Tawang in January. In other months, booking a day or two ahead by phone usually works.

sections.heading: Eating well for less
paras: Food is one of the easier budget wins. Momos, thukpa and noodle soups cost ₹80–180 in Tawang, Bomdila and Dirang; a rice meal with dal, vegetables and a meat curry costs ₹150–300 in most towns. Homestay dinners, already in your room rate, are often the best meals you will eat: in Monpa homes expect khura buckwheat pancakes, zan porridge and butter tea; in Apatani homes smoked pork, bamboo shoot and pike pila; in Adi homes river fish and greens.

Carry snacks and water for long Sumo days, as roadside stops can be short. Rice beer is offered as hospitality in many homes; it is fine to decline. Packaged food and bottled water cost more in remote areas such as Mechuka and Miao, so a refillable bottle and purification tablets save money and plastic.

sections.heading: Ten ways to spend less
paras: Most savings come from a few choices made before you leave home: when you travel, how you move between valleys and where you sleep. These are the ones that make the biggest difference on our saver trips.
list: Travel in March–April or November rather than peak October, when rooms and taxis cost more.
Apply for your e-ILP online before you travel instead of queuing at a check gate.
Book Sumo seats the evening before at the town counters; ask for a front seat on long days.
Choose homestays with dinner and breakfast included rather than hotels plus restaurants.
Share reserved taxis, such as the Tawang lakes day, with other guests; the vehicle price is fixed.
Stay longer in fewer places; every move costs a day of transport.
Take overnight trains to Guwahati, Naharlagun or Dibrugarh to save a night's room.
Carry enough cash from Guwahati, Tezpur or Dibrugarh; ATMs in small towns run dry.
Use a refillable bottle and purification tablets instead of buying water.
Pick one circuit per trip: Tawang, Ziro or the Siang. Combining them adds long, costly transfer days.

sections.heading: Costs people forget to plan for
paras: A few expenses catch budget travellers out. Monastery museums and some sanctuaries charge small entry and camera fees. Talle Valley, Daying Ering and Namdapha need forest permission, a guide and often a hired vehicle, which can add ₹3,000–6,000 to a day. Bum La, if you can get permission, needs a dedicated vehicle from Tawang.

The other hidden cost is time. Landslides in the monsoon and snow in winter can hold a road closed for a day or more, which means another night's room and food. Build one spare day into any trip, keep ₹3,000–5,000 in reserve, and book flights home with a margin rather than on the day you come down from the hills.

sections.heading: Sample budgets for two circuits
paras: For six nights on the Tawang circuit by shared Sumo, with homestays in Dirang, Tawang and Bomdila, a shared taxi for the high lakes and the e-ILP, plan on about ₹18,500 per person for two sharing, plus travel to Tezpur and lunches. Travelling alone, add about 25–40 percent for single rooms and unshared taxis.

For four nights in Ziro in an Apatani homestay, with Sumos from Itanagar, one day with a village guide and a shared taxi, plan on about ₹12,000 per person for two sharing. Festival dates in late September cost more. A week on the Siang and in Mechuka by Sumo costs roughly ₹22,000–28,000 per person, since the distances are longer. These are our indicative 2026 figures; check current fares and rates before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to visit Tawang?
faqs.a: Take a train or bus to Tezpur, then shared Sumos to Dirang and Tawang, staying in homestays with meals. Share a reserved taxi for the high lakes with other travellers. Six nights cost about ₹18,500 per person for two sharing, plus travel to Tezpur. Indicative 2026 figure.

faqs.q: How much does a Sumo cost in Arunachal?
faqs.a: Shared Sumo seats cost about ₹500–800 from Itanagar to Ziro, ₹700–1,000 from Tezpur to Dirang, and ₹1,100–1,500 from Tezpur to Tawang. Front seats sometimes cost a little more. Fares change, so check at the counter.

faqs.q: How much is the Inner Line Permit fee?
faqs.a: The tourist e-ILP costs a few hundred rupees, depending on the length of stay and current rules. Apply online on the official Arunachal government portal. Fees and rules change, so check current status before you travel.

Very few. Budget travellers mostly use homestays and simple guesthouses, which cost about ₹1,200–2,500 per person with meals or per double room without. Homestays often work out cheaper once meals are counted.

faqs.q: Is Arunachal more expensive than Sikkim or Himachal?
faqs.a: Usually a little, because distances are longer and there are fewer state buses and budget beds. Homestays with meals and shared Sumos keep costs close to other Himalayan states.

faqs.q: Do I need cash in Arunachal?
faqs.a: Yes. Towns like Tawang, Bomdila, Ziro and Pasighat have ATMs, but they can run dry, and many homestays and Sumo counters take only cash. Carry enough from Guwahati, Tezpur or Dibrugarh.

faqs.q: Can students travel in Arunachal on a tight budget?
faqs.a: Yes. With shared Sumos, homestays and local food, ₹2,500–3,000 a day per person is possible when two share. Travel in shoulder months and stay longer in fewer places.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to travel solo or in a group?
faqs.a: Groups of three or four save the most, since reserved taxis and rooms are shared. Solo travellers pay more for single rooms and unshared vehicles, roughly 25–40 percent extra.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest month to visit Arunachal?
faqs.a: March and November offer good weather with lower demand than peak October and May. The monsoon months are cheapest but bring landslides and road closures, so we do not recommend them for first trips.
